Architecture is the art and science of designing and constructing buildings and physical structures that serve human needs while embodying aesthetic, technical, and cultural values. Spanning from ancient temples to contemporary skyscrapers, it represents the intersection of practical engineering, artistic vision, and social purpose. Each era's architectural styles reflect its technological capabilities, economic priorities, and philosophical beliefs, shaping human experience by defining the spaces in which societies live, work, worship, and gather.

Architecture emerged as a formal discipline in ancient civilizations including Greece, Rome, and Egypt, where standardized proportional systems—the Five Classical Orders in the Greco-Roman tradition—were developed and transmitted across centuries. The built environment communicates cultural identity: Gothic cathedrals express medieval Christian spirituality, Islamic architecture incorporates geometric abstraction reflecting monotheistic principles, and Japanese temples employ natural materials reflecting Zen Buddhist aesthetics. Architectural movements correspond to historical periods and technological innovations. Romanesque and Gothic styles followed medieval social organization, Renaissance architecture revived Classical proportions, and Industrial-era building techniques enabled steel-frame skyscrapers impossible in earlier epochs.

Structural innovation drives stylistic change. The development of reinforced concrete, steel frames, and glass curtain walls freed architects from load-bearing walls, enabling open interior spaces and dramatic vertical forms. Architects function as intermediaries between clients' practical requirements and aesthetic or social ambitions, requiring technical training in materials science, structural analysis, and building codes alongside artistic sensibility. Functionalism—the principle that form should follow function—became a dominant twentieth-century philosophy, rejecting ornamental excess in favor of rational, efficient design. Urban planning and civic architecture profoundly shape social life, with architectural decisions encoding assumptions about community, privacy, mobility, and collective values.
